real_qa.q: What is a project bank account and how does it protect construction supply chains from contractor insolvency?
real_qa.r: A project bank account works by having the tier one contractor identify payments due to the supply chain, the client then pays monies into a ring-fenced bank account held under a trust arrangement. The trust protects the money from insolvency practitioners: if a tier one contractor goes insolvent, the trust prevents them from accessing the supply chain's money. The key advantage is that National Highways pays contractors, including subcontractors, within 18 days through project bank accounts, meaning less money is exposed to upstream insolvencies.
real_qa.requete: how project bank account protects construction subcontractors

real_qa.q: Why did New Mexico's 2007 ban on construction retentions fail and what workarounds did contractors use?
real_qa.r: The New Mexico legislation banning retentions in 2007 became ineffective because contractors found ways around it. Rather than explicitly taking retentions, they withheld sums of money earlier in the payment process by not paying full amounts, creating hidden retentions. Alternatively, they renamed retentions as bonuses—paying a bonus only on completion once satisfied with the work, which legally circumvents the ban.

real_qa.q: What are the government's proposed payment reforms for UK construction and what is the retention deposit scheme consultation?
real_qa.r: The government launched a consultation in July 2024 (closed October 2024) proposing to either abolish retentions or place retention money into ring-fenced accounts similar to a project bank account, modeled on the tenancy deposit scheme used for landlords. The government also proposes payment periods no longer than 60 days. However, a previous consultation on retentions in October 2017 received majority support for securing retention money via project bank accounts, but the government deemed there was no consensus and took no action.
real_qa.requete: UK government construction payment reform consultation 2024

real_qa.q: How much value has National Highways processed through project bank accounts and what payment speed have they achieved?
real_qa.r: National Highways has put through approximately 20 to 25 billion pounds worth of work through project bank accounts. They pay all their contractors, including subcontractors, within 18 days, demonstrating that project bank accounts enable faster payment cycles and provide protection by limiting exposure to at most the value of work in the current payment cycle.
real_qa.requete: National Highways project bank account 20 billion payment 18 days

real_qa.q: What threshold does Scotland and Wales use for mandatory project bank accounts in construction?
real_qa.r: Scotland and Wales mandate project bank accounts for construction projects valued at £2 million and above. Rudi Klein suggests this threshold could potentially be reduced to £1 million. Queensland, Australia has mandated project bank accounts for all construction projects regardless of value or sector.
real_qa.requete: Scotland Wales project bank account 2 million threshold mandate

real_qa.q: What happened to ISG and its supply chain in relation to the Ministry of Justice contracts?
real_qa.r: The Ministry of Justice appointed ISG, a tier one contractor with essentially no balance sheet and no cash, to deliver prison projects. ISG's collapse imperiled its supply chain. Though project bank accounts were in place on four prison projects, many companies found they were not paid because their payment applications were not processed. The case demonstrates the government had not learned from the Carillion collapse.
real_qa.requete: ISG Ministry of Justice prison projects collapse supply chain

guest.bio_context: Rudi Klein is a barrister and director of Klein Legal. He was formerly chief executive of the Specialist Engineering Contractors Group and has been a long-time campaigner for payment reform in the construction industry. He has been instrumental in promoting project bank accounts across Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, England, and Australia, and is currently advising Sable, a fintech company developing digital project bank account solutions.
